Simultaneous H2S mitigation and methanization enhancement of
chicken manure through the introduction of the micro-aeration
approach

a b s t r a c t
The impact on H2S alleviation and methane yield enhancement after submitting the anaerobic digestion
of chicken manure to a ﬁnite amount of air was investigated. The largest reduction in the H2S biogas
content (58% lower) occurred when air intensity of 30 ml/g VSin was injected into the reactors. Conse-
quently, a maximum methane yield (335 mL-g VSin
1), which was 77% higher than the control, was
concurrently achieved. Slight sulfate accumulation (<330 mg L1) was observed inside the micro-aerated
digesters with higher air intensities, suggesting a suppression of sulﬁde inhibition. Bacterial diversity/
richness was enhanced in these digesters while the relative abundance of Methanocelleus increased by
36%. The most important contributing factor to enhancement was the synergistic effect resulting from
increments in the hydrolysis rate and the suppression of sulﬁde inhibition. The results highlighted the
potential of in situ H2S mitigation with the added beneﬁt of methane yield enhancement.

In the last decade the amount of livestock manure in China has

rapidly increased, and it is estimated to reach 2.78 billon tons by the
year 2020 (Yan et al., 2017). This type of waste is both energy-rich
and bio-digestible, making anaerobic digestion (AD) an optimal
solution for its management (Anjum et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
However, the high content of sulfurous matter has been identiﬁed
as a barrier to livestock AD as it can induce the inhibition of
anaerobic microbes by H2S. Methionine, for instance, a sulfur-
containing amino acid, is nutritionally essential in feeding regime
for both laying hens and broiler chickens to support feather growth
and protein synthesis. Thus, chicken manure becomes rich in
sulfur-containing amino acids which their anaerobic digestion
forms sulfurous compounds. The presence of sulfurous compounds
in the AD concert highlights current challenges such as the out-
competition among indigenous organisms accompanied by these
compounds with methane producers resulting in the decreasing of
not only the quality but also the quantity of the biogas. At the same
time, the removal of H2S from biogas makes the whole AD process
less economical.
Speciﬁcally, sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) will be promoted in
the presence of organic matters and sulfates under anaerobic
condition where sulfate will be used as the terminal electron
acceptor and methanogenic substrates (acetate, H2) will act as
electron donors leading to H2S formation as the main product
(Reaction 1 and 2). H2S is toxic to methanogens at relatively low
concentrations. It is also highly reactive, has a bad odour, and is
corrosive to piping and equipments associated with the biogas in-
dustry. Extra investment costs are thus required in order to main-
tain the system (Krayzelova et al., 2015). On the other hand, in an
AD process, SRB will compete with methanogens to utilize electron
and this negatively affects the methane production. Various ap-
proaches have been put forward to mitigate the formation of H2S
during the AD process including chemical methods such as pre-
cipitation (Dhar et al., 2011), scrubbing (Couvert et al., 2008),
oxidation (Khanal and Huang, 2006), pH elevation (Yan et al., 2018),
and biological methods (Show et al., 2013). Nevertheless, even if
these techniques can remove H2S from biogas and thus increase the
quality and quantity of biogas production, the ﬁnal economic bal-
ance is still not positive.

Recent studies have demonstrated that micro-aeration could
provide an innovative solution for addressing the H2S issues
(Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). Micro-aeration refers to the addition of
a ﬁnite amount of air or oxygen into the anaerobic system to sup-
port a partial oxidation of H2S to elemental sulfur by sulﬁde-
oxidizing bacteria (Reaction 3) (Guerrero et al., 2016).

Micro-aeration could also have a positive impact on the overall
AD performance of the process, including hydrolysis efﬁciency
improvement, methane yield enhancement, and the scavenging of
hydrogen sulﬁde; however, other studies were more contradictory.
For instance, Botheju et al. (2010) demonstrated an enhancement in
the methane yield of starch by 30e55%, and Tertakovsky et al.
(2011) increased the methane yield of synthetic wastewater by
26% after adding limited oxygen to anaerobic digesters. However,
Ramos et al. (2014) and Diaz et al. (2011) reported a negligible
impact of micro-aeration on the process performance of sewage
sludge and the methane yield of cellulose, respectively. Overall, a
wide range of H2S removal efﬁciency, from 30% to more than 99%,
has been reported in the literatures (Zhou et al., 2007; Krayzelova
et al., 2014; Fdz-Polanco et al., 2009); therefore, more accurate
knowledge about micro-aeration optimization i.e., air intensity
(Tsapekos et al., 2017) could help clarify these variations and
maximize the potential application of this approach.
In addition to this, the dynamic of the microbial community in
micro-aerated AD reactors is also not quite clear. Some studies have
reported that micro-aeration has no strong impact on the dynamics
of microorganisms (Tang et al., 2004) while other studies have
stated that micro-aerated systems have a higher diversity and
relative abundance of hydrolytic microorganism, i.e. Firmicutes,
compared to a strict AD system (Yin et al., 2016). Lim et al. (2014)
have reported a 14% enhancement in the relative abundance of
Firmicutes in a micro-aerated system compared to a strict AD one. In
addition to the diversity, methanogenic activity has, on occasion,
been found to improve more under micro-aeration conditions in
comparison to the conventional AD system (Fu et al., 2016). How-
ever, it has also been demonstrated that methanogenic activity
inhibition depends more on sulﬁde concentration than micro-
aeration (Jenicek et al., 2011a, 2011b). While Brioukhanov and
Netrusov (2007) reported the suppression of SRB growth and ac-
tivity by oxygen. Jenicek et al. (2011a, 2011b) found that SRB ac-
tivity was not negatively affected under micro-aeration conditions,
and the activity of sulﬁde-oxidizing bacteria was signiﬁcantly
enhanced. Such a technology is affected by many other factors and
these are often referred in the relevant literature (Nguyen and
Khanal, 2018). Accordingly, it seems likely that although several
studies have been performed to elucidate the role of providing
microaerobic environment into AD treating different organic
wastes, controversial results have been reported. Furthermore, to
our knowledge, the underlying mechanisms of the potential impact
of micro-aerated approach in terms of microbial dynamics,
methane production, hydrolysis performance and H2S reduction
have not been addressed concurrently. Therefore, a devoted
investigation to entirely evaluate and deﬁne the potential impact of
micro-aeration approach in the entire AD process is necessary.
The current study, therefore, aimed to estimate the role of a
micro-aeration strategy in H2S removal, hydrolysis performance
and methane yield enhancement. Chicken manure batch AD re-
actors were supplemented with different air dosages and the H2S
removal efﬁciencies and methane yields of the different trials were
assessed.16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed to determine if,
and to what extent the micro-aeration strategy would shape the
proﬁle of the microbial community structure.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
The substrate used in this study was chicken manure and was
obtained from an egg-laying farm belonged to China Agriculture
University. The large particles i.e. feathers, were separated and then
the manure was sieved to avoid a blockage of tools and kept at 4 C
until usage. The fed chicken manure had a TS, volatile solid (VS),
and total chemical oxygen demand (TCOD) of 10%, 7% and 104 g/L
respectively. Sludge from a long-term laboratory-scale mesophilic
(37 C) digester fed with chicken manure was used as inoculum,
and this had a TS and VS content of 4.3% and 2.2% respectively. The
total volatile fatty acids in the inoculum were 300 mg L1 and the
total ammonium-nitrogen was 3982 mg L1. The inoculum digester
was operated consecutively for more than 90 days and the inoc-
ulum was thus well acclimated through the long term operation.
The chemical characteristics of the sludge (inoculum) and chicken
manure (substrate) are presented in Table S1 (supplementary
material).

2.2. Batch assays experimental setup
All batch experiments were carried out in sealed glass serum
bottles with a 70 and 120 mL working and total volume, respec-
tively. The chicken manure and sludge were mixed to reach a
substrate/inoculum ratio of 20/80 (volatile solids basis). The batch
digesters were instantly ﬂushed with N2 to provide harsh anaerobic
conditions. The butyl rubber stoppers and aluminum seals were
utilized to seal the digesters which were at mesophilic conditions
(37 ± 1 C). The micro-aeration treatments were carried out in the
ﬁrst 15 days of digestion using a syringe to inject air. Five sets of
micro-aerated reactors were set up: S1, S2, S3, S4 and S5 with air
intensity of 7, 10, 20, 30 and 50 mL/g VSin, respectively (Table 1). A
set of batch reactors were also used without applying micro-
aeration (S0). Additionally, blank digesters (sludge and water)
were used to quantify the amount of methane production by
inoculum (indigenous respiration). A total of 96 batch digesters
were set up (14 replicates for each trial). In order to measure
different parameters, two reactors from each trial were terminated
every 2e3 days in the ﬁrst 10 days of the experiment and then
every 5 days until the end of the experiment. All the experiments
were run until the methane production ceased. The methane pro-
duction was calculated at standard temperature and pressure
conditions.
2.3. Kinetic model
The ﬁrst-order kinetic model was used as equation (4):
ln ðCs0 = CsÞ ¼ kt
(4)
where Cs0 refers to the highest biogas production (mL); Cs stands
for the highest biogas production after subtracting the biogas cu-
mulative (mL); k is the rate constant of the ﬁrst order (day1); t is
the elapsed time (day).
2.4. H2S and sulfate monitoring
Sulfate in the digestate was measured by Ion Chromatography
ICS-3000 (method: HJ/T84-2001). Hydrogen sulﬁde concentrations
were measured (using test kits of Gastec, No, 4H; 104000 ppm) in
the reactors with and without air injection to calculate the effect of
micro-aeration on H2S removal (H2S removal efﬁciency, RH2S) using
equation (5) according to (Choudhury et al., 2019):
2.5. Analytical measurements
2.5.1. Analytical measurements
Total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), total chemical oxygen de-
mand (TCOD) and ammonia (NH4þ-N) were analyzed according to
standard methods (APHA 2005). Soluble parameters were deter-
mined after centrifugation of the samples at 10,000 rpm for 10 min
(Cence TGL-16 M, China) and these were then ﬁltered through a
0.22 mm ﬁlter. Gas composition was measured with Gas Chroma-
tography
(Sp-2100)
consisting
of
a
stainless-steel
column
(10 m  2 mm) at 0.4 MPa hydrogen pressure and a speed of
60 ml min1. Inlet, column oven and TCD temperatures were 130,
130, 116 C, respectively. VFAs were analyzed by Gas Chromatog-
raphy (Shimadzu GC-2010 plus, Japan) consisting of detector (ﬂame
ionization) and column (RTX-wax). The methane values were
normalized to standard conditions (1.01 bar and a temperature of
273.2 K). The pH variation was determined using the Mettler-
Toledo pH meter.
2.5.2. Microbial analysis
DNA extraction from the samples was performed using the
cetyltrimethyl
ammonium
bromide/sodium
dodecyl
sulfate
method. Universal primers 338F/806R for bacteria sequences and
524F/958R for archaeal sequences were utilized for PCR ampliﬁ-
cations. Denaturation at 98 C (for 1 min, followed by 30 cycles for
10s), annealing at 50 C (for 30 s), and elongation at 72 C (for 30 s
and then 5 min) were the major properties of the thermal cycling of
PCR. The amplicons were sequenced using NEB Next® Ultra™DNA
Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, USA). The Qubit@ 2.0 Fluorom-
eter (Thermo Scientiﬁc) with Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system and
the Illumina HiSeq
platform were
used for evaluating and
sequencing the library quality, and then the reads were merged
with FLASH.
The data was explored using the Quantitative Insights Into Mi-
crobial Ecology software package (QIIME), and alpha- and beta-
were processed using in-house Perl scripts. QIIME quality ﬁlters
and pick_de_novo_otus.py were also applied for reads ﬁltration and
creating an OTU table. Consequently, Chao1, Simpson and Shannon
indices were calculated.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. The effect of micro-aeration injection on H2S mitigation
The cumulative emission of H2S in biogas when the micro-
aeration technology was applied is illustrated in Fig. 1. The cumu-
lative emission of H2S in the control digesters (10,400 ppm) was

used as a baseline to determine the efﬁciency of H2S removal in
micro-aerated AD. The achieved desulfurization efﬁciency in micro-
aerated AD was between 28% and 58% (Fig. 1b). However, even
though the sulﬁde concentration decreased noticeably, not all the
sulﬁde was removed from the biogas. It is clear, nevertheless, that
the accumulation of H2S decreased with the increase in air in-
tensity. The highest H2S removal efﬁciency was observed in micro-
aerated AD with an air intensity of 30 mL/g VSin. Conversely, no
distinct improvement was observed when air intensity increased to
50 mL/g VSin (S5), indicating that the air intensity at this level may
be was over the oxidation capacity of sulﬁde oxidizers and/or the
relative abundance of SRB was not sufﬁcient to utilize all available
O2 and H2S. Indeed, a slightly reduction of H2S removal efﬁciency
was even observed at highest air intensity when comparing with
air intensity at 30 mL/g VSin, implying that the air was not supplied
suitably. This evidence demonstrated that air intensity at 30 mL/g
VSin could be used as a crucial threshold to improve H2S mitigation
in the process. Therefore, increasing air intensity up to 30 mL/g VSin
helped to enhance the removal efﬁciency of H2S by improving the
activity of sulﬁde-oxidizing bacteria. As H2S is the outcome of SRB
activity, this reduction in accumulative H2S may also be due to SRB
inhibition. It has been reported that oxygen at relatively low con-
centrations could exert toxic effects on sulfate reducers through
formation of reactive species and competition with the electron-
accepting sulfate, thus blocking dissimilatory sulfate reduction or
inactivation of their enzymes (Brioukhanov and Netrusov 2007).
The highest H2S removal efﬁciency attained in this study (58%) was
comparably 2-fold higher than that achieved by Zhou et al. (2007)
(Table 2).
On the other hand, the sulfate concentration in the efﬂuent of
the micro-aerated digesters was always higher than that found in
the control (Fig. 2). Furthermore, the sulfate content rose along
with the increase in the air intensity which may be attributed
somewhat to sulﬁde oxidation. The former phenomenon could also
be occurred as a result of suﬁdogenesis limitation, and this meant
that sulfate reduction either did not continue occur at all or
occurred to a limited extent. Consequently, methanogenic sub-
strates were more available for methanogens. In return, this limi-
tation most probably led to the enhancement of methanogens
which had resulted from the H2S mitigation. In addition, the rela-
tive abundance of hydrogenotrophic methanogens, with particular
reference to Methanocellus, as shown in the next section, increased
signiﬁcantly in the micro-aerated systems. The relationship be-
tween SRB and methanogens activities on electron donors has been
reported in a previous study (Damianovic and Foresti 2009).
Therefore, the increase in the sulfate concentration can be
explained by the maintenance of high methanogenic activity,
which thus resulted in higher methane yields inside micro-aerated
digesters. Remarkably, the sulfate levels in all the micro-aerated
reactors (47e326 mg L1) were far below the inhibition threshold
of methanogens. Mizuno et al. (1994) reported methanogenesis
inhibition at a sulfate concentration of 1600 mg L1. However,
higher sulfate removal was achieved in the control AD since this
removal resulted in the production of H2S in the biogas, and this
could partially explain the higher H2S content in its biogas
(10,400 mg L1) (Fig. 3). Nevertheless, a dedicated study in
continuous reactors to completely monitor the fate of sulfurous
compounds and S mass balance in micro-aerated systems is highly
necessary.
3.2. Methane yield enhancement with micro-aeration
The methane yields of the control (S0) and micro-aerated AD (S1,
S2, S3, S4 and S5) of chicken manure are shown in Fig. 3. As depicted,
the methane yields of S0, S1, S2, S3, S4 and S5 were 190, 265, 278, 292,
335 and 199 mL/g VSin, respectively, indicating that the methane
yields obviously improved in the micro-aerated AD reactors. A
possible reason for this enhancement could be due to the sup-
pression of the inhibition caused by sulﬁde as discussed above. The
highest methane yield was achieved when the air intensity was
30 mL/g VSin, which was 77% higher than that from the digesters in
the control AD. The results revealed that the methane yield rose
along with the increase in air intensity up to 30 mL/g VSin, implying
that the injected air up to that level was maintained below the
inhibition threshold. These results are in agreement with Tsapekos
et al. (2017) who reported a micro-aeration intensity over 10 mL O2/
gVS may induce the anaerobic process’ disturbances. Likewise, Fu
et al. (2016) reported that increasing the air load to more than
12.5 mL/LR-d did not lead to a higher methane yield when corn
straw was digested. Subsequently, increasing the air intensity up to
50 mL air/g VSadded in this study resulted in a sharp drop in the
methane yield. A similar outcome was also observed by Xu et al.
(2014), and the reason could be that over-aeration maybe beyond
the oxygen consumption and/or anti-oxidation capacity of facul-
tative
bacteria
which
resulted
in
detrimental
effects
on
methanogens.
In fact, several studies have demonstrated a profound effect on
AD process performance when a small amount of air or oxygen is
supplemented into the AD process; however, the enhancement
achieved in the present study was higher than those achieved
before (Table 2). For instance, Tsapekos et al. (2017) reported a 7.2%
enhancement in the methane yield of wheat straw when 5 mLO2/g
VS was supplemented in the AD system for 3 days while Lim and
Wang (2013) reported a 21% enhancement in the methane yield
of brown water and food waste in micro-aerated AD (37.5 mLO2/LR-
d for 4 days) compared to methane yields attained in a strict AD
system (Table 2). These results, and the results attained in this
study, highlight how substrate characteristics could have a pro-
found effect on micro-aeration strategy. For instance, chicken

manure is rich in both ammonia (as depicted in Table S1, supple-
mentary material) and sulfur-containing amino acids and the
synergistic co-inhibition effect of sulﬁde and ammonia on anaer-
obic digestion has been recently reported in literature (Surmeli
et al., 2017). It is, however, worth noting that the sulfur com-
pounds, NH3 and VFA levels, the results of degradation of certain
substrates, i.e., chicken manure, could provide an appropriate
environment for H2S production and methanogenesis inhibition,
and thus the outcome and the positive impact of micro-aeration
strategy on the process would vary accordingly which will be
more pronounced with such substrates.

the digestion time. As depicted, lower VFA concentrations were
observed in micro-aerated systems compared to the control AD
which was similar to trends reported in previous studies (Jenicek

et al., 2011a, 2011b; Diak et al., 2013). Acetate represented almost
all VFAs in the systems with highest air intensities (S3, S4 and S5),
indicating that the applied air intensity in these digesters did not
provoke a vital shift to undesired higher redox potentials as longer
fatty acids, i.e., propionate are preferred in less anaerobic envi-
ronments with higher redox conditions (Sawatdeenarunat et al.,
2015). Conversely to the control digester, as can be seen in Fig. 3,
acetate represented all, or at least the highest proportion, of the
VFAs in the micro-aerated digesters regardless of air intensity. This
also indicated that the micro-aeration procedure promoted the
degradation or oxidation of the unusable or less appropriate VFAs
from methanogens as concluded by Tsapekos et al. (2017). The
current results are in agreement with previous studies that dealt
with different substrates in which the application of micro-aeration
in the AD process decreased the accumulation of more complex
VFAs (Lim and Wang 2013; Tsapekos et al., 2017). It was this that
most likely contributed to the higher methane yields attained in the
micro-aerated AD compared to the control AD.
In addition, the ﬁrst-order kinetic model, which is commonly
applied to simulate biodegradability as a result of microbial activity
in the AD process, was used for comparison between both systems.
The value of hydrolysis kinetics obtained by the ﬁrst-order model
demonstrated that the reaction rate was maximized under micro-
aerobic conditions (Fig. 4). This veriﬁed the enhancement of the
methane yield after the micro-aeration strategy as a result of
increasing substrate availability to acidogens to produce VFAs for
subsequent stages. Acceleration in hydrolysis kinetics resulted in
60% enhancement in hydrolysis efﬁciency after 4 days in the micro-
aerated system (Johansen and Bakke, 2006). This enhancement
may be attributed to the enhancement of extracellular enzymes
excretion of facultative microorganisms which may have favored
the presence of oxygen. More speciﬁcally, Gibb’s free energy (DG0,
KJ/e) of different VFAs (including valerate, butyrate, propionate
and acetate) conversions are thermodynamically unfavorable
(þ12.1) and favorable (106.7) under anaerobic and micro-aerobic
conditions, respectively (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). Therefore, the
reason behind this enhancement was that facultative bacteria were
most probably favored to shift their metabolic pathway from
anaerobic fermentation to aerobic respiration which is more
thermodynamically.
3.3. Bacteria diversity, richness, and structure with air injection
The richness and diversity indices of bacteria and archaea
communities are shown in Fig. 5. The results indicated that the
micro-aeration strategy increased the abundance of the bacteria
community as the Choa index was higher in the micro-aerated AD
compared to the control AD. Furthermore, the higher Shannon in-
dex (4.2 vs 3.8) and the lower Simpson index (0.03 vs 0.05) in the
micro-aerated system demonstrated that the microbial community
with micro-aerated digesters was also more diversiﬁed than that in
the control AD system. Indeed, it has been reported that micro-
aeration could establish more diverse functional groups (hydro-
lytic and fermentative bacteria) with higher activity than the strict
AD system (Lim et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2016).
In both systems, the most predominant phylum was Firmicutes,
accounting for 47e48% of total reads, followed by Bacteroidetes
(36e37%) and Cloacimonetes (6e8%) which are the most frequent
bacterial sequences reported in the anaerobic digestion process
(Lee et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2018). These results differ from that
reported by Fu et al. (2016) who demonstrated that the relative
abundance of Firmicutes, with particular reference to Clostridiales,
rose under micro-aeration conditions. However, the relative
abundance of members belonging to Proteobacteria increased by
32% under micro-aerobic conditions. It has been previously re-
ported that the majority of SRB and sulﬁde-oxidizing bacteria
belong to Proteobacteria (Krayzelova et al., 2015; Pokorna and
Zabranska 2015). Given the fact that the methane yield was
enhanced, and hydrolysis kinetics was accelerated in the micro-
aerated system, it seems likely that even if there were no varia-
tions in the phyla proportions among the systems, bacterial rich-
ness and diversity were different, as illustrated above. Furthermore,
the bacterial activity may be altered as well. In fact, it has been
reported that the growth rate of acetogens decreased considerably
under oxidative stress without affecting acetate synthesis activity
(Brioukhanov and Netrusov 2007). An anaerobic microenviron-
ment, where the methanogens are protected, could be provided
through the oxygen uptake of such bacteria (Kato et al.,1993) as the
success of the micro-aeration strategy relies mainly on the oxygen
consumption of facultative bacteria that belong to these phyla.
Only those genera with remarkable differences in relative
abundance between both systems are shown in Fig. 6a. Among the
highly abundant bacteria, Fastidiosipila, Proteiniphilum, Alkaliphilus
Choacamonas, Caldicoprobacter and Syntrophomonas decreased
remarkably when shifting from the strict AD to the micro-aerated
AD, indicating less tolerance of oxygen. The relative abundance of
norank_o_MBAO3,
noranck_o_M55-D21,
norank_f_Syn-
trophomonadaceae and Gelria almost doubled in the micro-aerated
system. However, most of them corresponded to uncultured, un-
classiﬁed, and unranked bacteria and thus their roles in micro-
aerated systems were uncertain. Gelria, however, was the excep-
tion and it has been proposed that species belonging to Gelria play a
signiﬁcant role in producing hydrogen, and thereby support their
hydrogenotrophic methanogens partners (Lu et al., 2014). In this
study, three genera of SRB, namely Desulfobulbus and Desulfovibrio
(Proteobacteria) and Desulﬁtibacter (Firmicutes), were identiﬁed in
the control digesters at a relatively low abundance (<1%) and their
existence was further decreased by half in the micro-aerated AD.
These genera are commonly known as SRB genera in sulfate
reduction reactors and belong to the incomplete organic oxidizers
(Hao et al., 2014). Species belonging to Desulfobulbus and Desulfo-
vibrio have been found to utilize ethanol, lactate and hydrogen as
electron donors, and sulfate as electron acceptors to produce ace-
tate (incomplete oxidizing SRB) (Liu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018).
The decrease in relative abundance of H2-utilized SRB might be
compensated by the increase in relative abundance of H2-utilized
methanogens. On the other hand, many species of sulfur oxidizing
bacteria, such as Thioalkalimicrobium, Halothiobacillus, Paracoccus
and Pseudomonas (Friedrich et al., 2001; Sorokin and Kuenen 2005;
Vikromvarasiri and Pisutpaisal 2014), were found in the micro-
aerated AD at relatively low abundance and these were presumed
to be responsible for higher hydrogen sulﬁde removal efﬁciency.

3.4. Archaea richness, diversity, and structure with air injection
Contrary to the results obtained with the bacteria (Fig. 4), both
the richness and diversity of archaea decreased in the micro-
aerated AD compared to the control AD (Fig. 4). This indicates
that only oxygen tolerant archaea survived in the micro-aerobic
regime and thus a more specialized archaea community was
assembled. These ﬁndings are consistent with a previous study
which declared that microbiome clustering was signiﬁcantly
inﬂuenced by micro-aeration strategy (Ramos et al., 2014).
The archaeal community is depicted in Fig. 6b, and Meth-
anoculleus was the most predominant methanogens in both sys-
tems; however, its relative abundance in micro-aerated digesters
was 36% higher than that of the control. This result was in accor-
dance with a pervious study (Fu et al., 2016) which found Meth-
anocelleus was the prevalent methanogens under microaerobic
conditions. Methanocelleus is a hydrogenotrophic methanogens
which produces methane through the reduction of CO2 using H2 as
an electron donor (Barret et al., 2013). The increase in relative
abundance of such genus most probably led to the rise in hydro-
genotrophic methanogenesis rather than hydrogenotrophic sulﬁ-
dogenesis, resulting in the slight accumulation of sulfate in the
micro-aerated system (Fig. 2). This result was in accordance with
Tang et al. (2004) who observed that the Methanoculleus population
increased with micro-aeration strategy when the analysis of 16S
rRNA genes and quantitative real-time PCR were applied. The
acetoclastic methanogen Methanoseate, on the other hand, were
found but in relatively low abundance (2.3%) in the control AD, and
the decreased (<1%) in the micro-aerated AD. The abundance of
hydrogenotrophic
methanogens
and
the
lack
of
acetoclastic
methanogens suggests that methane creation was through a two-
stage acetate conversion by the syntrophic acetate oxidizing bac-
teria coupled with hydrogenotrophic methanogens (SAO-HM)
(Westerholm et al., 2010). Indeed, even though there is an absence
of oxygen tolerance in most methanogens in pure culture, this
tendency may be changed in mixed culture such as the culture of
anaerobic digestion process. Under mixed culture, facultative bac-
teria could potentially protect intolerant methanogens from oxygen
exposure. Therefore, the enhancement in bacterial diversity and
richness that was achieved in the current study (Fig. 5) was the
most important contributing factor in methanogens tolerance for
oxygen.
4. Conclusion
The simultaneous suppression of sulﬁde toxicity and the
enhancement of the methane yield (77% higher) using micro-
aeration technology in order to upgrade the biogas production of
chicken manure, were the main ﬁndings of the current study.
Proper air intensity (30 ml/g VSin) led to the highest H2S removal
(58%) and the maximum methane yield enhancement. The richness
and the diversity of bacteria were enhanced and the archaeal
Methanocelleus exclusively became the dominant methanogens in
the new environment. This study supports the proposal that
